cues.text:
I have two timestamps on this example
pull request.

The author marked it ready at ten on
Monday. The first teammate commented on
the code at two on Tuesday.

The team counts business hours, so with
a nine-to-five schedule that is seven

hours on Monday and five on Tuesday,
twelve in all.

The baseline across forty requests is
eighteen business hours.

This measurement starts at readiness. It
tells the manager where work is waiting
after the author has asked for a review.

Try tracing the same two points on a
pull request from your team.

Suppose reviewers say small fixes are
hard to pick up when the expected
outcomes are buried in the ticket.

The pilot gives every eligible change a
focused diff, clear boundary tests,
and a short summary.

Copilot helps the author prepare that
package. Ask for a prediction the team
can check.

We expect those pull requests to reach
their first substantive review sooner.

Write an eligibility rule and try two
examples. The zero-quantity issue
qualifies.

A database migration with several
services and design decisions keeps its
usual process.

Set aside four weeks for the baseline
and four for the pilot.

Use the same service and the same
definition of an eligible fix in both
windows.

Keep a small table of the task mix and
which reviewers covered the queue each
week.

Suppose the pilot's third week had an
extra reviewer.

Flag it in the scorecard. That coverage
could contribute to the result.

This is a useful pilot design for a
local decision.

A historical comparison leaves several
explanations open,

so save the context and bring it to the
review meeting.

Agree on how to count before you start
measuring.

A substantive first review discusses the
change.

A bot result or an acknowledgment such
as ‘looking soon’ leaves the clock
running.

Active review minutes measure time spent
reading and evaluating the pull request.

Material rework means the author has to
change an important part of the proposed
behavior, tests, or scope.

A spelling suggestion is a different
kind of feedback.

Give reviewers two sample comments and
have them label each one.

Compare answers so the team starts with
a common definition.

The team sets the finish line before the
results arrive.

Median wait should drop from eighteen
business hours to fourteen or less.

Active review starts at twenty-four
minutes,

and the team allows three additional
minutes.

Twenty-four plus three gives us a
twenty-seven minute limit.

The rework ceiling is fifteen percent
and the spending cap is three hundred
dollars.

Track post-merge defects with a fixed
follow-up period.

A serious data or access incident
triggers a pause and the agreed response
process.

Put these rules where the decision owner
can find them.

The engineering lead is accountable for
the pilot record.

The author and reviewer own their parts
of each pull request.

Use issue seventeen and pull request
forty-two as the walkthrough.

Read the change, check the times, and
ask who would label a rework request.

Schedule a quick weekly check to catch
missing evidence while the team can
still recover it.

Before starting, hand the record to a
teammate.

Ask them to explain which tasks qualify,
when the review clock starts,

and what result would make the team
pause.
Fix anything they interpret differently.
